implementation_notes: Ktor publishes the protocol through nested routing (routing { route("/v1/orders") { post { ... } } }) with ContentNegotiation and kotlinx.serialization, so exactly the types marked @Serializable are the wire contract and the mapping from domain types to those DTOs is the translation layer; nothing else is serialised. Versioning is a route prefix or an Accept media type, and the contract document comes from Ktor's OpenAPI plugin or a checked-in spec. Kotlin makes the seam cheap - data classes for DTOs, internal visibility for domain modules - but the serializer annotations are the contract: marking a domain class @Serializable is the same act as publishing it.
pitfalls: @Serializable on a domain class publishes its whole structure (including @SerialName renames); keep serializers on DTO classes only.

kotlinx.serialization encodes or omits default values according to the Json{} configuration, so a single encodeDefaults/explicitNulls change alters the wire shape - pin the Json instance next to the contract.
internal visibility protects modules inside one compilation, not a published artifact: shipping the domain module itself exposes it.
